replacement: “Gentlemen of the jury,” began the prosecutor, “this case has caused a stir all over Russia. But why should that surprise us? What is so especially horrifying in it for us? We are so used to such crimes! That is what is truly horrible: that such dark deeds no longer horrify us. What ought to horrify us is that we have grown so used to them, and not this or that single crime. What are the causes of our indifference, of our lukewarm attitude toward such deeds, toward such signs of the times, which are ominous for an unenviable future? Is it our cynicism? Is it the premature exhaustion of mind and imagination in a society that is sinking into decay in spite of its youth? Is it that our moral principles are shattered to their foundations, or perhaps that we have no such principles at all? I cannot answer such questions. Yet they are disturbing, and every citizen not only must, but ought to be troubled by them. Our newborn and still timid press has already done the public good service, for without it we would never have heard of the horrors of unbridled violence and moral degradation that the press keeps bringing to the notice, not only of those who attend the new jury courts set up in the present reign, but of everyone. And what do we read almost every day? Of things beside which the present case grows pale and seems almost commonplace. But what matters most is that the majority of our national crimes of violence bear witness to a widespread evil, now so general among us that it is hard to fight against it.

“Then he met a young girl of lofty character and brilliant education. Oh, I do not venture to repeat the details; you have only just heard them. There was honor there, and self-sacrifice, and I will say no more. The young officer, frivolous and profligate, paying homage to true nobility and a lofty ideal, showed himself to us in a very sympathetic light. But the other side of the coin was turned toward us without warning right afterwards, in this very court. Again I will not venture to guess why it happened so, but there were reasons. The same lady, in tears of long-concealed indignation, stated that he, of all men, had despised her for her action. That action was rash, even reckless perhaps, but it was still prompted by lofty and generous motives. He, the girl’s betrothed, looked at her with that smile of mockery, which was harder to bear from him than from anyone. And knowing that he had already deceived her (he had deceived her, believing that she was bound to put up with anything from him, even betrayal), she purposely offered him three thousand roubles. She made it clear, too clear, that she was offering him the money so that he would deceive her. ‘Well, will you take it or not? Have you no shame left?’ was the silent question in her searching eyes. He looked at her and saw plainly what she was thinking (he has admitted before you that he understood it all). He took that three thousand without any conditions, and squandered it in two days with his new sweetheart.
